newsitem.title: UK: OPEC president contacts ministers over price slide.
newsitem.headline: OPEC president contacts ministers over price slide.

text.p: OPEC President Libyan Oil Minister Abdalla el-Badri has consulted on the telephone with his ministerial counterparts to discuss the slide in world oil markets, OPEC sources said on Wednesday.

"There has been some contact this week. He (Badri) was planning to call all the ministers," said an OPEC delegate. "There is concern about prices but as things stand there is nothing more than that," the delegate said.

Ministers in the Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries have watched the value of their crude oil exports dive some 30 percent since the turn of the year putting renewed pressure on national budgets.
Benchmark London Brent futures have slumped nearly $7 a barrel to $18 from an early January high and physical crude sales are discounted by a further dollar.
OPEC delegates and officials said the group remains extremely unlikely to take any action ahead of their next scheduled conference in Vienna on June 25.
"No one is planning anything at OPEC, that's for sure," said a senior OPEC official last week.
"There is nothing serious being considered," said a delegate.
Seven or eight ministers from the 11-member group will get the chance to exchange views on the turnaround in the oil market at an oil and gas conference in Iran in May.
OPEC's output quota compliance committee has scheduled a regular quarterly meeting in Isfahan, Iran on May 6-7 ahead of a conference arranged by the National Iranian Oil Corp (NIOC) for May 8-10.
The committee, chaired by Iranian Oil Minister Gholamreza Aghazadeh, also comprises Nigeria's Dan Etete and Indonesia's Ida Bagus Sudjana. OPEC Secretary-General Rilwanu Lukman also will attend.
NIOC says it also expects Kuwaiti Oil Minister Isa al-Mazeedi, Qatar's Abdullah bin Hamad al-Attiyah and the UAE's new Oil Minister Obaid bin Saif al-Nasseri for the conference.
Libya's el-Badri also is expected to attend and Venezuela's Erwin Arrieta has expressed interest, NIOC conference organisers said.
OPEC kingpin Saudi Oil Minister Ali al-Naimi will not go to Isfahan.
OPEC's biggest producer, having enjoyed a $12 billion budget windfall from unexpectedly high oil prices last year, raised its 1997 budget projection for a barrel of Saudi crude by $2 to $16-$16.50.
Main Saudi export stream Arab Light on Wednesday was valued at just $15 for European buyers, down from $23 in January.
Nigeria set a $17 barrel price assumption for 1997 versus $16 for 1996. Nigerian crude currently is valued at about $17.
Even when OPEC meets in June its options for defending oil prices look severely limited, OPEC delegates and analysts said.
OPEC output has increased faster than expected this year, hitting 26.90 million barrels a day (bpd) in March compared to an official 25.03 million ceiling, according to a Reuters survey.
OPEC's Gulf trio of Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and the UAE still have capacity in hand but supply restraint seems a thing of the past for most of the remainder of the group.

"Commercial considerations are now ingrained for most OPEC members," said one member country official. "There's simply no going back to the days when OPEC tried to support prices and left non-OPEC to walk away with increased market share."
"OPEC no longer reacts to price changes," said analyst Geoff Pyne at finance house UBS in a recent report.
Increasingly the main body of OPEC producers, fuelled by foreign oil company investments, are behaving like their non-OPEC counterparts and producing to capacity.
Venezuela leads the way, now tipping the scales at 3.18 million bpd or 35 percent above its official quota.
Qatar, at 560,000 bpd is nearly 50 percent above its much smaller quota.
"These countries should respect their quotas," said an OPEC official. "Without that there is no chance of any response from those abiding by their quotas."
